supplement.holds: Search strategies, brainstorming instructions, tool design requirements, workshop demographics (Table 9), model identifiers and prompts, task cards and screenshots, annotation interface, semantic-distance plots (Figure 14), and supplementary results by brainstorming method (Tables 10-11).

paper_design_summary: University and company volunteers participated in a human-only formative study (12 people), an Initial AI co-design study (16), and a main Final AI versus no-AI evaluation (54), which comprised chatbot-companion and medical-AI workshop sets (PDF p. 3, Figure 2). Teams brainstormed benefits, risks, and mitigations using structured or free-form methods, and experts rated the generated outputs for novelty, plausibility, and other quality dimensions (PDF pp. 9-11, section 5, Tables 2 and 4). Participants registered and were assigned to groups with balanced backgrounds, but the allocation procedure for AI assistance is unstated; design_class is other because neither random nor explicitly non-random condition assignment is established (PDF pp. 7-8, section 4).

participants.who: Volunteers recruited from universities and companies through mailing lists and posters in Cambridge, Oxford, and London; private-sector workers, researchers, and students with at least a bachelor's degree. Individuals, rather than existing teams, were recruited, and each could attend only one workshop (PDF pp. 7-8, section 4). The paper labels the ten evaluation workshops as one main study with 54 people: 29 in the chatbot-companion set and 25 in the medical-AI set (PDF p. 3, Figure 2). The count here is the people in those completed workshops, not the expert raters. Section 5.1 says outputs from all 15 workshops were rated; the exact participant subset entering the Table 4 models is not separately specified.

task.description: Teams acted as company developers and generated benefits, risks, and mitigations for either the Salieri chatbot companion or ArcLight kidney monitoring/transplant allocation application. They ideated, organized impacts, and proposed mitigations using Futures Wheel, Empathy Mapping, or Free-form brainstorming; Free-form was used only in the chatbot evaluation set (PDF pp. 7-9, sections 4-5; p. 26, Table 9; p. 32, Appendix F).
task.duration: 80 minutes of brainstorming: 45 minutes ideate, 15 minutes converge, 20 minutes decide (PDF p. 3, Figure 2, Step 3).

outcomes.name: Novelty of benefits, risks, and mitigations
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: AI versus No AI, stratified by use case and impact type. Novelty is rated on a 1-3 scale from mundane to imaginative. Table 4A reports CLM means ± SE, back-transformed to Likert values: chatbot benefits 2.02* ±.16 versus 1.90* ±.05; chatbot risks 1.83 ±.11 versus 1.80 ±.03; chatbot mitigations 1.86 ±.11 versus 1.83 ±.03; medical benefits 1.93 ±.22 versus 2.01 ±.06; medical risks 1.80 ±.18 versus 1.70 ±.05; medical mitigations 1.79 ±.20 versus 1.68 ±.05. The table marks chatbot-benefit novelty as significant (* p < .05, Tukey-adjusted), whereas section 5.3 says creativity measures did not improve; this discrepancy is unresolved. The paper does not state whether individual ratings or aggregated impact scores constitute the CLM observations, so unit is null.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 10, Table 2 and sections 5.1-5.2; p. 11, Table 4A, Novelty column and section 5.2 continuation; p. 12, section 5.3, Finding 1.

outcomes.name: Plausibility of benefits, risks, and mitigations
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: AI versus No AI, stratified by use case and impact type. Plausibility is an expert rating on a 1-5 scale. Table 4A reports CLM means ± SE: chatbot benefits 4.08** ±.15 versus 3.82*** ±.07; chatbot risks 3.86*** ±.10 versus 3.56*** ±.05; chatbot mitigations 3.94*** ±.11 versus 3.31*** ±.05; medical benefits 3.66 ±.21 versus 3.73 ±.09; medical risks 3.70 ±.17 versus 3.65 ±.09; medical mitigations 3.70 ±.19 versus 3.56 ±.10. Stars are retained exactly as printed (** p < .01; *** p < .001, Tukey-adjusted); medical plausibility cells carry no significance marks. The CLM observation unit is not specified, so unit is null.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 10, Table 2 and sections 5.1-5.2; p. 11, Table 4A, Plausibility column and significance legend; p. 12, section 5.3, Finding 1.

outcomes.name: Number of generated impacts (benefits, risks, and mitigations)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: AI versus No AI. Section 5.3 reports 48% more impacts for the chatbot companion and 22% more for medical AI. Table 4A separately prints Count: chatbot benefits 68 versus 29, risks 96 versus 80, mitigations 78 versus 54; medical benefits 33 versus 27, risks 46 versus 42, mitigations 59 versus 29. These are counts of generated impacts, not people. The table does not explain the aggregation of Count across workshops or provide count-specific uncertainty; unit is null. The derivation of the prose percentages is not supplied; the medical 22% statement and the printed counts are retained without reconciliation or calculation of a replacement effect.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11, Table 4A, Count column; p. 12, section 5.3, Finding 1.

outcomes.name: Uniqueness of benefits, risks, and mitigations
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert rating on a 1-3 scale. Table 2 asks: "Is this {benefit/risk/mitigation} unique to this specific AI use?" This measures specificity to the particular AI use. The paper calls it a creativity measure alongside Novelty (PDF p. 12, section 5.3, Finding 1), but it is a separate rating and does not measure diversity across people. Section 5.1 says five expert annotators from a pool of 90 rated each impact from all 15 workshops. The exact workshop subset in Table 4A and whether the CLMs use individual ratings or aggregated impact scores are not specified; analysis unit and n_units remain null. The reported arm means have SEs, not SDs; statistics_available records the printed significance thresholds.

contrasts.reported: AI versus No AI, stratified by use case and impact type. Table 4A reports CLM estimated marginal means ± SE, back-transformed to Likert values: chatbot benefits 1.99 ±.18 versus 1.88 ±.06; chatbot risks 1.89 ±.11 versus 1.87 ±.03; chatbot mitigations 1.86 ±.11 versus 1.87 ±.03; medical benefits 1.90* ±.23 versus 2.09 ±.06; medical risks 1.96** ±.18 versus 1.75 ±.05; medical mitigations 1.89 ±.20 versus 1.80 ±.06. Significance marks are copied exactly as printed: * p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001 (Tukey-adjusted). The medical-benefit AI cell carries * and the medical-risk AI cell carries **; their corresponding No AI cells have no stars. Chatbot uniqueness cells are unstarred. The medical-benefit estimate is lower with AI and the medical-risk estimate is higher; section 5.3 highlights the latter.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 10, Table 2 (Uniqueness) and sections 5.1-5.2; p. 11, Table 4A (Uniqueness column) and section 5.2 continuation; p. 12, section 5.3, Finding 1.

outcomes.name: Probability of benefits, risks, and mitigations
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert rating on a 1-7 scale. Table 2 asks: "How likely is this {benefit to be realised / risk to occur / mitigation to be implemented}?" This rates the likelihood that the described benefit is realised, risk occurs, or mitigation is implemented; it is not an overall creativity rating. Section 5.1 says five expert annotators from a pool of 90 rated each impact from all 15 workshops. The exact workshop subset in Table 4A and whether the CLMs use individual ratings or aggregated impact scores are not specified; analysis unit and n_units remain null. The reported arm means have SEs, not SDs; statistics_available records the printed significance thresholds.

eligibility.reason: Re-evaluated after adding the omitted output ratings and reviewing Figure 14. The full text, including appendices, does not state random assignment or an explicit non-random allocation of AI assistance. Participants registered for workshops and were assigned to groups, with backgrounds balanced (PDF pp. 7-8, section 4); criterion 1 remains unclear. The paper labels its ten evaluation workshops as one main study with 54 people, comprising separate chatbot and medical sets of 29 and 25 (PDF p. 3, Figure 2 and contribution (3)); criterion 2 uses that main-study total. Expert output ratings include novelty and the separately recorded task-specific uniqueness measure, so criterion 3 remains met (PDF p. 10, Table 2 and section 5.1; p. 11, Table 4A). Core eligibility remains unclear pending clarification of assignment, the use-case sample grouping, and whether Table 4A includes formative/co-design outputs, since section 5.1 describes rating all 15 workshops. Figure 14 labels AI-generated versus human-generated outputs without defining the human pool or an assistance contrast (PDF p. 35; p. 36, Appendix H); it does not resolve assignment or establish a separate ai_vs_human context sample. No observational context classification is established without a stated non-random allocation; context_class remains none.

one_line_finding: AI-assisted teams produced chatbot risks with higher rated plausibility (3.86 ±.10 versus 3.56 ±.05) but similar novelty (1.83 ±.11 versus 1.80 ±.03), with limited medical-task gains and unstated randomization (CLM mean ± SE; PDF p. 11, Table 4A; p. 12, section 5.3; p. 8, section 4).
notes: Supplementary semantic-distance result, retained here and excluded from assistance-effect outcomes: Figure 14 (PDF p. 35; Appendix H, opening paragraph on p. 36) compares AI-generated with human-generated benefits, risks, and mitigations using Cosine Distance (1 - cosine similarity). All three panels print "Mann-Whitney U: p < 0.05"; the plotted AI-generated distributions have lower cosine distances. These are output-origin labels, not an established comparison of AI-assisted versus unassisted human teams, so the figure does not establish an across_people assistance effect. The embedding model, which outputs or pairs were compared, analysis unit, sample sizes, exact U statistics, numerical group summaries, and confidence intervals are not specified; none are inferred from the plot. The human-generated pool is not identified as exclusively unassisted, so this figure alone also does not establish the codebook’s ai_vs_human context class. Appendix H, Table 10 reports these output-quality scales by brainstorming method; those method comparisons are not additional AI-assistance contrasts.
